claim: Ventral anterior temporal lobes (vATL) form a deep hub in a broadly distributed cortical semantic network that coordinates activation amongst various surface representations.
source: The ventral anterior temporal lobes (vATL) form a deep hub in this network that coordinates activation amongst the various surface representations (Patterson et al., 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Patterson et al., 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017).

claim: The vATL acquires distributed representations that allow the semantic network to express conceptual similarity structure, supporting inductive generalization of acquired knowledge across conceptually related items.
source: In so doing, the vATL acquires distributed representations that allow the whole network to express conceptual similarity structure, supporting inductive generalization of acquired knowledge across conceptually related items (Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Rogers et al., 2004).

claim: Many researchers view semantic representations of visually-presented objects as arising from the propagation of activity upward through a feature hierarchy, beginning with simple perceptual features and ending with abstract cross-modal features.
source: Many researchers view such representations as arising from the propagation of activity upward through a feature hierarchy, beginning with simple perceptual features, moving through intermediate modality-specific features, and ending with abstract cross-modal features that express semantic category structure.
evidence: The claim describes a perspective held by many researchers in the field, representing established knowledge in the domain.

claim: The feature hierarchy perspective has strongly influenced computational models of object recognition developed in visual neuroscience and associated brain imaging work.
source: This perspective has strongly influenced computational models of object recognition developed in visual neuroscience (Isik et al., 2014; Serre et al., 2007) and associated brain imaging work (Cichy et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior works (Isik et al., 2014; Serre et al., 2007; Cichy et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte, 2015).

claim: Semantic representations may arise from interactive settling processes within distributed and dynamic brain networks.
source: Alternatively, semantic representations may arise from interactive settling processes within distributed and dynamic brain networks (Patterson et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Patterson et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2017).

claim: On the distributed and dynamic view, semantic representations are activation patterns encoded jointly over many neural populations, with similar concepts evoking similar patterns.
source: On this view, semantic representations are activation patterns encoded jointly over many neural populations, with similar concepts evoking similar patterns.
evidence: The claim describes a theoretical perspective on semantic representation.

claim: In distributed and dynamic semantic representations, the information encoded by a given population depends on the states of other populations.
source: The information encoded by a given population depends on the states of other populations, so that the whole representation is best viewed as a point in a multidimensional state space (Rogers and McClelland, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Rogers and McClelland, 2004).

claim: Stimulus processing in distributed and dynamic semantic systems involves a transitioning through multidimensional state space as the system settles toward an interpretation of the input.
source: Stimulus processing involves a transitioning of the system through the space, rather than the activation of increasingly abstract/complex feature detectors, as the whole system settles toward an interpretation of the input (Rogers and Patterson, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Rogers and Patterson, 2007).

claim: Many models of semantic memory adopt the distributed and dynamic perspective.
source: Many models of semantic memory adopt this perspective (Chen et al., 2017; Farah and McClelland, 1991; Cree et al., 1999; Harm and Seidenberg, 2004; Plaut and Shallice, 1993), which also aligns with the general view that the ventral visual processing stream is recurrent and interactive (Kravitz et al., 2013; Goddard et al., 2016; Kietzmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior works (Chen et al., 2017; Farah and McClelland, 1991; Cree et al., 1999; Harm and Seidenberg, 2004; Plaut and Shallice, 1993; Kravitz et al., 2013; Goddard et al., 2016; Kietzmann et al., 2019).

claim: On feature-based views, local populations of neurons independently encode the presence of a particular feature.
source: On featured-based views, local populations of neurons independently encode the presence of a particular feature, licensing a straightforward interpretation of neural activity: when the population is active, the corresponding feature has been detected, inferred, or called to mind; when inactive, it hasn't.
evidence: The claim describes a theoretical perspective on neural representation.

claim: If semantic representations are distributed, the local behavior of a single population may not be interpretable independent of the others.
source: If, however, semantic representations are distributed, the local behavior of a single population may not be interpretable independent of the others (Cox et al., 2014); and if semantic processing is also dynamic, the contribution of a local population to the distributed code may change in real time, potentially in highly nonlinear ways (Mante et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cox et al., 2014; Mante et al., 2013).

claim: If semantic processing is dynamic, the contribution of a local population to the distributed code may change in real time, potentially in highly nonlinear ways.
source: If, however, semantic representations are distributed, the local behavior of a single population may not be interpretable independent of the others (Cox et al., 2014); and if semantic processing is also dynamic, the contribution of a local population to the distributed code may change in real time, potentially in highly nonlinear ways (Mante et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Mante et al., 2013).

claim: Treatment of neurophysiological signals as arising from independent feature detectors can mischaracterize how neural systems encode semantic information if representations are distributed and dynamic.
source: These possibilities suggest that the treatment of neurophysiological signals as arising from independent feature detectors can mischaracterize how neural systems encode semantic information.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the preceding discussion about distributed and dynamic representations.

claim: In the hypothetical example shown in Figure 1, two neural populations jointly encode semantic information at every timepoint, but the contribution of each changes over time.
source: The categories are always well differentiated, so the two populations jointly encode semantic information at every timepoint, but because the trajectories are nonlinear each population's contribution to this structure changes over time—the category discrimination plane rotates.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of Figure 1 and the figure itself.

claim: Independent correlation analysis of neural populations can lead to incorrect conclusions about when and how semantic information is represented if the code is distributed and dynamic.
source: Independent correlations suggest conclusions about when and how semantic information is represented that are incorrect under the distributed and dynamic view.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis presented in Figure 1B and the accompanying text.

claim: Discovery of distributed and dynamic semantic codes requires neural data with high temporal and spatial resolution.
source: First, spatial and/or temporal averaging can obscure signal if the code truly is distributed and dynamic—discovery requires neural data with high temporal and spatial resolution, ruling out the non-invasive methodologies that constitute the majority of work in this area (Contini et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Contini et al., 2017) and logical inference about the requirements for detecting such codes.

claim: Discovery of distributed and dynamic semantic codes requires multivariate methods because independent univariate analysis can mischaracterize information distributed across multiple channels.
source: Second, independent univariate analysis can mischaracterize information distributed across multiple channels—discovery requires multivariate methods (Grootswagers et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Grootswagers et al., 2017).

claim: Studies connecting neurophysiological measurements to computational models of visual recognition have primarily focused on feed-forward models that do not exhibit dynamic processing.
source: Third, studies connecting neurophysiological measurements to computational models of visual recognition have primarily focused on feed-forward models that do not exhibit dynamic processing (Cichy et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cichy et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2015).

claim: Some recent decoding evidence suggests visual processing in ventral temporal cortex is dynamic.
source: While some recent decoding evidence suggests visual processing in ventral temporal cortex is dynamic (Kietzmann et al., 2019), no prior work has assessed how representations evolve within distributed and dynamic semantic models, and consequently it is unclear what this view predicts or how it differs from feature-based approaches.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Kietzmann et al., 2019).

claim: No prior work has assessed how representations evolve within distributed and dynamic semantic models.
source: While some recent decoding evidence suggests visual processing in ventral temporal cortex is dynamic (Kietzmann et al., 2019), no prior work has assessed how representations evolve within distributed and dynamic semantic models, and consequently it is unclear what this view predicts or how it differs from feature-based approaches.
evidence: The claim represents a gap in the literature identified by the authors.

claim: The study combined computational modeling, multivariate pattern classification, and electrocorticography (ECoG) to assess whether semantic representations in human vATL are distributed and dynamic.
source: We therefore combined computational modeling, multivariate pattern classification, and electrocorticography (ECoG) to assess whether semantic representations in human vATL are distributed and dynamic.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology of the current study.

claim: The study focused on vATL due to its central role in semantic representation.
source: We focused on vATL due to its central role in semantic representation (Patterson et al., 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017) and because it is a common target for grid implantation in patients awaiting surgery to remediate epilepsy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Patterson et al., 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017).

claim: vATL is a common target for grid implantation in patients awaiting surgery to remediate epilepsy.
source: We focused on vATL due to its central role in semantic representation (Patterson et al., 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017) and because it is a common target for grid implantation in patients awaiting surgery to remediate epilepsy.
evidence: The claim represents clinical knowledge about epilepsy surgery procedures.

claim: Nonlinear dynamics arise in a well-studied neurocomputational model of semantic memory.
source: We first showed that the nonlinear dynamics highlighted in our thought experiment arise in a well-studied neurocomputational model of semantic memory (Rogers et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2017), then used temporal generalization of pattern classifiers (King and Dehaene, 2014) to establish the predicted 'signature' of a dynamically changing semantic code (is the stimulus animate or inanimate?) under this model.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results presented in the paper and citations to prior work (Rogers et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2017).

claim: Temporal generalization of pattern classifiers can establish the predicted 'signature' of a dynamically changing semantic code.
source: We first showed that the nonlinear dynamics highlighted in our thought experiment arise in a well-studied neurocomputational model of semantic memory (Rogers et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2017), then used temporal generalization of pattern classifiers (King and Dehaene, 2014) to establish the predicted 'signature' of a dynamically changing semantic code (is the stimulus animate or inanimate?) under this model.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methodology described and a citation to prior work (King and Dehaene, 2014).

claim: The critical decoding signature predicted by the model was found in intracranial local field potentials collected from the surface of the left vATL while participants named line drawings of common items.
source: We next applied this technique to intracranial local field potentials collected from the surface of the left vATL while participants named line drawings of common items, and found the critical decoding signature—providing strong evidence that, at the level of spatiotemporal resolution captured by ECoG, the animacy of a visually depicted item is expressed in vATL by a distributed code that changes dynamically with stimulus processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by the ECoG data analysis presented in the paper.

claim: At the level of spatiotemporal resolution captured by ECoG, the animacy of a visually depicted item is expressed in vATL by a distributed code that changes dynamically with stimulus processing.
source: We next applied this technique to intracranial local field potentials collected from the surface of the left vATL while participants named line drawings of common items, and found the critical decoding signature—providing strong evidence that, at the level of spatiotemporal resolution captured by ECoG, the animacy of a visually depicted item is expressed in vATL by a distributed code that changes dynamically with stimulus processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by the ECoG data analysis presented in the paper.

claim: The neural code exploited by classifiers changed over time and across the ventral temporal surface.
source: Finally we considered how the neural code exploited by classifiers changed over time and across the ventral temporal surface, with results that reconcile the two divergent views of semantic representation in the brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of classifier coefficients presented in the paper.

claim: The results reconcile the feature-based and distributed-dynamic views of semantic representation in the brain.
source: Finally we considered how the neural code exploited by classifiers changed over time and across the ventral temporal surface, with results that reconcile the two divergent views of semantic representation in the brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: The hub and spokes model of semantic memory is a fully continuous and recurrent neural network that learns cross-modal associations between distributed visual and verbal representations via three reciprocally connected hidden layers.
source: The model was a fully continuous and recurrent neural network that learns cross-modal associations between distributed visual and verbal representations via three reciprocally connected hidden layers (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim describes the architecture of the computational model used in the study, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The trained hub and spokes model settles to an attractor state representing any item specified by the input.
source: Activity propagates in both directions, from surface representations to hub and back, so that the trained model settles to an attractor state representing any item specified by the input.
evidence: The claim describes the behavior of the trained model.

claim: The model was trained to complete patterns representing ninety items from three model conceptual domains, each organized into three categories containing ten items.
source: We trained the model to complete patterns representing ninety items from three model conceptual domains (e.g. animals, objects, and plants), each organized into three categories containing ten items (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: The claim describes the training procedure for the model.

claim: Items from different categories in the same domain shared a few properties while those in the same category shared many.
source: Items from different categories in the same domain shared a few properties while those in the same category shared many.
evidence: The claim describes the structure of the training data for the model.

claim: The 3D MDS of hub activation patterns shows a systematic but nonlinear elaboration of the conceptual structure latent in the stimulus patterns.
source: The result in Figure 2B shows a systematic but nonlinear elaboration of the conceptual structure latent in the stimulus patterns: the domains separate from one another early on, but each item follows a curved trajectory over the course of stimulus processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by the visualization shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The curved trajectories in the model's representational space are not an artifact of data-reduction.
source: The curves are not an artifact of data-reduction—Figure 2C shows these trajectories in the native activations of randomly-sampled unit pairs in one network run, where they are clearly nonlinear (and see A-1 for comparative results with linearly-changing representations).
evidence: The claim is supported by the visualization shown in Figure 2C and reference to Appendix A-1.

claim: Independent correlation analysis of each hub unit's behavior produces mixed results, with some units behaving like tonic category detectors, some like transient detectors, some appearing to flip their category preference, and others appearing not to code category information at all.
source: Consequently, independent correlation analysis of each unit's behavior produces mixed results (Figure 2D), with some behaving like tonic category detectors (green squares), some like transient detectors (blue), some appearing to flip their category preference (red) and others appearing not to code category information at all (gray).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The full distributed pattern across hub units elaborates conceptual structure from early in processing, but the progression is nonlinear and only clearly discernable in a low-dimensional embedding of the space.
source: Thus, the full distributed pattern across hub units elaborates conceptual structure from early in processing, but the progression is nonlinear and only clearly discernable in a low-dimensional embedding of the space.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from the model simulations.

claim: Multivariate logistic classifiers can decode semantic category information from hub activation patterns in simulated ECoG data.
source: We therefore used multivariate logistic classifiers to decode semantic category information from hub activation patterns and assessed their behavior on simulated ECoG data, taking unit activation as a model proxy for the potential measured at a subdural electrode.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used to analyze the model data.

claim: For each simulated participant, a sparse random subsample (15%) of all hub units was selected, analogous to the sparse sampling of field potentials provided by a cortical sensor array.
source: For each simulated participant, we selected a sparse random subsample (15%) of all hub units—analogous to the sparse sampling of field potentials provided by a cortical sensor array—and recorded their responses to each stimulus at every tick of time.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used to simulate ECoG data from the model.

claim: Classifiers fitted to the model's hub activations performed well above chance as soon as input activation reached the hub units and throughout the time window.
source: Figure 3A shows the cross-validated accuracy at each timepoint averaged over many network runs and subsamples. The classifiers performed well above chance as soon as input activation reached the hub units and throughout the time window.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Classifiers fitted to earlier activation patterns in the model generalized only to immediate temporal neighbors, while those fitted to later patterns generalized over a wider window but failed at decoding earlier states.
source: Classifiers fitted to earlier activation patterns generalized only to immediate temporal neighbors, while those fitted to later patterns generalized over a wider window but failed at decoding earlier states (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the temporal generalization analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The temporal generalization profile of classifiers in the model exhibits an 'overlapping waves' pattern.
source: To better visualize these results, we clustered the rows of the matrix in Figure 3B and plotted the mean accuracy of the classifiers in each cluster across time (Figure 3C). The results exhibit an 'overlapping waves' pattern: classifiers that work on early patterns quickly fail at later timepoints where a different classifier succeeds.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: As time progresses in the model, the classifier clusters include more classifiers and the breadth of time over which the classifiers perform well widens.
source: As time progresses, the clusters include more classifiers and the breadth of time over which the classifiers perform well widens (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The overlapping waves pattern in the model reflects the nonlinear trajectories in the sparsely-sampled representational space as the network settles to an attractor state.
source: This pattern reflects the nonlinear trajectories apparent in the sparsely-sampled representational space as the network settles to an attractor state.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: When trajectories curve in representational space, earlier classification planes fail later in time while later planes fail at earlier time-points.
source: When trajectories curve, earlier classification planes fail later in time while later planes fail at earlier time-points.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the relationship between curved trajectories and classifier performance.

claim: If representations simply moved linearly from initial to final state, early classifiers would continue to perform well throughout processing.
source: If representations simply moved linearly from initial to final state, early classifiers would continue to perform well throughout processing—a pattern observed in simulations with feature-based models, models with distributed representations that evolve linearly, and recurrent but shallow neural networks (see A-1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative simulations described in Appendix A-1.

claim: In the deep network model, the non-linear dynamic pattern was observed only in the hub layer—in more superficial layers, the code remained stable.
source: In the deep network, the non-linear dynamic pattern was observed only in the hub layer—in more superficial layers, the code remained stable (A-2).
evidence: The claim is supported by additional simulations described in Appendix A-2.

claim: Distributed and dynamic semantic representations can arise in deep layers of interactive networks.
source: The simulations thus suggest that distributed and dynamic semantic representations can arise in deep layers of interactive networks and a deep, distributed, and dynamic semantic code of this kind will elicit a particular 'signature' when multivariate pattern classifiers are used to decode a binary semantic property such as animacy from ECoG data.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: A deep, distributed, and dynamic semantic code will elicit a particular 'signature' when multivariate pattern classifiers are used to decode a binary semantic property such as animacy from ECoG data.
source: The simulations thus suggest that distributed and dynamic semantic representations can arise in deep layers of interactive networks and a deep, distributed, and dynamic semantic code of this kind will elicit a particular 'signature' when multivariate pattern classifiers are used to decode a binary semantic property such as animacy from ECoG data.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The ECoG dataset included voltages collected at 1000 Hz from 16 to 24 subdural electrodes situated in the left ventral anterior temporal cortex of 8 patients awaiting surgery while they named line-drawings of common animate and inanimate items.
source: The dataset included voltages collected at 1000 Hz from 16 to 24 subdural electrodes situated in the left ventral anterior temporal cortex of 8 patients awaiting surgery while they named line-drawings of common animate and inanimate items matched for a range of confounds (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim describes the ECoG dataset used in the study.

claim: Voltages in the ECoG study were analyzed over the 1640ms following stimulus onset.
source: We analyzed voltages over the 1640ms following stimulus onset, a window that allows us to assess decodeability both before and after the mean onset of naming (1190 ms).
evidence: The claim describes the analysis window for the ECoG data.

claim: Voltages in the ECoG study were decoded using a 50 ms sliding-window, with separate classifiers fitted at each window and the window advancing in 10 ms increments.
source: Voltages were decoded using a 50 ms sliding-window, with separate classifiers fitted at each window and the window advancing in 10 ms increments.
evidence: The claim describes the decoding methodology for the ECoG data.

claim: The classifiers in the ECoG study were logistic regression models trained to discriminate animate from inanimate items based on the voltages measured across all electrodes.
source: The classifiers were logistic regression models trained to discriminate animate from inanimate items based on the voltages measured across all electrodes and for all time-points within the corresponding window.
evidence: The claim describes the classifier methodology for the ECoG data.

claim: Hold-out accuracy in the ECoG study exceeded chance at about 200 ms post stimulus onset, well before name initiation, and remained statistically reliable throughout the time window.
source: Hold-out accuracy exceeded chance at about 200 ms post stimulus onset, well before name initiation, and remained statistically reliable throughout the time window (Figure 4A) with no obvious change at the mean time of naming onset.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 200 ms in the ECoG study, classifiers generalized well to timepoints near the training window but poorly to more distal timepoints, with the generalization envelope widening as time progressed.
source: At 200 ms classifiers generalized well to timepoints near the training window but poorly to more distal timepoints, with the generalization envelope widening as time progressed (4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the temporal generalization analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The temporal generalization profile of classifiers in the ECoG study exhibited an 'overlapping waves' pattern strikingly similar to the simulation.
source: We again clustered the classifiers based on their temporal accuracy profile, then plotted mean profiles for each cluster (4 C). The result was an 'overlapping waves' pattern strikingly similar to the simulation: classifiers that performed well early in processing quickly declined in accuracy, replaced by a different well-performing set.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Over time in the ECoG study, neighboring classifiers began to show similar temporal profiles, forming larger clusters that performed above chance for a broader temporal window.
source: Over time neighboring classifiers began to show similar temporal profiles, forming larger clusters that performed above chance for a broader temporal window (4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In mid-posterior regions of ventral temporal cortex, the neural code for animacy was spatially and temporally stable.
source: In mid-posterior regions, the code was spatially and temporally stable—weights on the lateral aspect were positive while those on the medial aspect were negative, consistent with feature-based views of representation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of classifier coefficients shown in Figure 4E and Video 1.

claim: The stable code in mid-posterior regions is consistent with feature-based views of representation.
source: In mid-posterior regions, the code was spatially and temporally stable—weights on the lateral aspect were positive while those on the medial aspect were negative, consistent with feature-based views of representation.
evidence: The claim is an inference connecting the observed pattern to theoretical views.

claim: The anterior pattern of classifier coefficients differed from the posterior pattern, flipping from mainly positive at 200 ms to mainly negative by 800 ms and fluctuating across time and space throughout.
source: The anterior pattern differed, flipping from mainly positive at 200 ms to mainly negative by 800 ms and fluctuating across time and space throughout.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of classifier coefficients shown in Figure 4E and Video 1.

claim: The 'meaning' of a positive deflection in the voltage stayed constant posteriorly but changed direction over time anteriorly.
source: In other words, the 'meaning' of a positive deflection in the voltage—whether it signaled animal or non-animal—stayed constant posteriorly but changed direction over time anteriorly, consistent with the deep, distributed, dynamic view (see A-3).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the analysis of classifier coefficients.

claim: The fluctuating anterior pattern is consistent with the deep, distributed, dynamic view of semantic representation.
source: In other words, the 'meaning' of a positive deflection in the voltage—whether it signaled animal or non-animal—stayed constant posteriorly but changed direction over time anteriorly, consistent with the deep, distributed, dynamic view (see A-3).
evidence: The claim is an inference connecting the observed pattern to theoretical views.

claim: From 200 ms post-onset, 95% confidence intervals on mean decoding accuracy exceed chance for the duration of the stimulus-processing window in the ECoG data.
source: Figure 4A confirms this characteristic: from 200 ms post-onset, 95 % confidence intervals on mean decoding accuracy exceed chance for the duration of the stimulus-processing window.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 'overlapping waves' pattern shown in Figure 4C is statistically reliable across subjects.
source: To assess whether the 'overlapping waves' pattern shown in Figure 4C is statistically reliable across subjects we conducted the following analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Each cluster of classifiers in the ECoG study is reliably better than all other clusters at some point in time, excepting only the first and the last.
source: Each cluster is reliably better than all other clusters at some point in time, excepting only the first (classifiers fit to early windows that never exceed chance) and the last (which performs comparably to the second-last cluster toward the end of the processing window).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The generalization window in the ECoG study grows wider over the first ~500 ms of processing, where it hits a ceiling, then drops off for classifiers near the very end.
source: The generalization window grows wider over the first ~500 ms of processing, where it hits a ceiling (ie classifiers generalize above chance for almost the whole window) then drops off for classifiers near the very end.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The best piecewise-linear model of generalization window width in the ECoG study involved a single breakpoint at ~473 ms post stimulus onset.
source: From this approach, the best model involved a single breakpoint at ~473 ms post stimulus onset.
evidence: The claim is supported by the piecewise-linear regression analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The first segment of the piecewise-linear model shows a reliable linear widening of the generalization window with fit time over ~500 ms (r2 = 0.70, p < 0.002).
source: The first model segment shows a reliable linear widening of the generalization window with fit time over ~500 ms (r2 = 0.70, p < 0.002), providing strong evidence that the generalization window expands linearly with stimulus processing until it hits ceiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the piecewise-linear model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Classifier coefficients fluctuate more over time in anterior than posterior temporal cortex.
source: The surface maps shown in Figure 4E and accompanying animation (Video 1) suggest that classifier coefficients fluctuate more over time in anterior than posterior temporal cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by the visualization shown in Figure 4E and Video 1.

claim: Anterior/posterior location predicts variance of coefficient change with r2 = 0.73, P < 0.002.
source: The result is shown in Figure 5C: anterior/posterior location predicts VoC with r2 = 0.73, P < 0.002.
evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Across participants, the slope relating variance of coefficient change to anterior/posterior location was reliably positive (t(7) = 2.58 vs null hypothesis of zero slope, p < 0.02 one-tailed).
source: Across participants this slope was reliably positive (t(7) = 2.58 vs null hypothesis of zero slope, p < 0.02 one-tailed), indicating greater fluctuation of classifier coefficients in more anterior regions across participants.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis across participants.

claim: At the scale of intracranial EEG, neural signals throughout ventral temporal lobe jointly express animacy information from about 200 ms post stimulus-onset.
source: The results suggest that, at the scale of intracranial EEG, neural signals throughout ventral temporal lobe jointly express such information from about 200 ms post stimulus-onset, via a distributed code that is stable and feature-like in middle/posterior regions but dynamic and nonlinearly-changing in anterior regions.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The neural code for animacy is stable and feature-like in middle/posterior regions of ventral temporal lobe but dynamic and nonlinearly-changing in anterior regions.
source: The results suggest that, at the scale of intracranial EEG, neural signals throughout ventral temporal lobe jointly express such information from about 200 ms post stimulus-onset, via a distributed code that is stable and feature-like in middle/posterior regions but dynamic and nonlinearly-changing in anterior regions.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Similar phenomena to those observed in ECoG arise in a deep, interactive neuro-semantic model.
source: In simulation we showed that similar phenomena arise in a deep, interactive neuro-semantic model, producing a characteristic decoding signature: classifiers perform well in the time-window when they were trained, but generalize over a narrow time envelope that widens as the system settles.
evidence: The claim summarizes the simulation findings.

claim: The overlapping waves pattern was only observed in a model combining distributed representation, interactive processing, and a deep architecture.
source: This pattern was only observed in a model combining distributed representation, interactive processing, and a deep architecture (see Appendix).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative simulations described in the Appendix.

claim: The results support the proposal that vATL encodes distributed semantic representations that change dynamically and nonlinearly with stimulus processing by virtue of this region's role as a deep hub within the cortical semantic network.
source: Remarkably similar phenomena were observed in ECoG data collected from the surface of ventral temporal lobe while participants named line-drawings, supporting the proposal that vATL encodes distributed semantic representations that change dynamically and nonlinearly with stimulus processing by virtue of this region's role as a deep hub within the cortical semantic network.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the combined simulation and ECoG results.

claim: Convergent methods have established the centrality of vATL for semantic memory.
source: Convergent methods have established the centrality of vATL for semantic memory, including studies of semantic impairment (Julie et al., 1989; Hodges et al., 1995; Lambon Ralph et al., 2007), lesion-symptom mapping (Acosta-Cabronero et al., 2011 ), functional (Visser et al., 2010; Rogers et al., 2006) and structural (Binney et al., 2012; Binney et al., 2010) brain imaging, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (Pobric et al., 2010; Pobric et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Multivariate approaches to discovering neuro-semantic representations rarely identify the vATL, instead revealing semantic structure more posteriorly.
source: Yet multivariate approaches to discovering neuro-semantic representations rarely identify the vATL, instead revealing semantic structure more posteriorly (Bruffaerts et al., 2013; Devereux et al., 2013; Sha et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Bruffaerts et al., 2013; Devereux et al., 2013; Sha et al., 2015).

claim: One prominent study suggested that semantic representations may tile the entire cortex except for the vATL.
source: One prominent study suggested that semantic representations may tile the entire cortex except for the vATL (Huth et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Huth et al., 2016).

claim: Almost all multivariate studies of semantic representation have employed non-invasive imaging techniques that sacrifice either temporal or spatial resolution.
source: Setting aside significant technical challenges of successful neuroimaging of this region (Binney et al., 2010), almost all such studies have employed non-invasive imaging techniques that sacrifice either temporal or spatial resolution—a compromise that will destroy signal in vATL if semantic representations there are distributed and dynamic at the scale we have measured, but will preserve signal in posterior regions where the code is more stable.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Binney et al., 2010) and represents knowledge about neuroimaging methods.

claim: The widespread null result in multivariate studies may arise precisely because semantic representations in vATL are distributed and dynamic.
source: Thus the widespread null result may arise precisely because semantic representations in vATL are distributed and dynamic.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the current findings and prior literature.

claim: Several fMRI studies have reported category effects in the mid-posterior fusiform, with animate items eliciting greater activation on the lateral bank and inanimate items eliciting greater activation on the medial bank.
source: Several fMRI studies have reported category effects in the mid-posterior fusiform, with animate items eliciting greater activation on the lateral bank and inanimate items eliciting greater activation on the medial bank (Martin and Chao, 2001; Anzellotti et al., 2011; Mahon et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies (Martin and Chao, 2001; Anzellotti et al., 2011; Mahon et al., 2009).

claim: In the current study, mid-posterior fusiform regions are where a stable, feature-like code arises, with animate items signaled by positive voltages on the lateral aspect and negative voltages on the medial aspect.
source: In our analysis, these are regions where a stable, feature-like code arises, with animate items signaled by positive voltages on the lateral aspect and negative voltages on the medial aspect.
evidence: The claim connects the current findings to prior fMRI results.

claim: Because the location and direction of the code are more stable in mid-posterior regions within and across subjects, the signal remains detectable even with the spatial and temporal averaging that occurs in univariate fMRI.
source: Since the location and direction of the code are more stable in these regions within and across subjects, the signal remains detectable even with the spatial and temporal averaging that occurs in univariate fMRI.
evidence: The claim is an inference explaining why fMRI detects signals in posterior but not anterior regions.

claim: When multiple channels are affected by a common source of noise, multivariate decoders can place weights on uninformative channels that 'subtract out' the noise corrupting the signal on informative channels.
source: When multiple channels are affected by a common source of noise, multivariate decoders can place weights on uninformative channels that 'subtract out' the noise corrupting the signal on informative channels (Haufe et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Haufe et al., 2014).

claim: Classifiers trained on only the anterior electrodes in each participant showed reliable decoding.
source: First, we fit classifiers to only the anterior electrodes in each participant and observed reliable decoding—indeed, performance was equally reliable for classifiers trained on anterior-only and posterior-only datasets (A-4).
evidence: The claim is supported by additional analysis described in Appendix A-4.

claim: Performance was equally reliable for classifiers trained on anterior-only and posterior-only datasets.
source: First, we fit classifiers to only the anterior electrodes in each participant and observed reliable decoding—indeed, performance was equally reliable for classifiers trained on anterior-only and posterior-only datasets (A-4).
evidence: The claim is supported by additional analysis described in Appendix A-4.

claim: An earlier study applied searchlight representational similarity analysis (RSA) to the same data and found that vATL was the only local region that reliably encodes semantic similarity structure.
source: Second, an earlier study applied searchlight representational similarity analysis (RSA) to the same data (Chen et al., 2016), and found that vATL was the only local region that reliably encodes semantic similarity structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2016).

claim: The observed pattern of a stable code posteriorly and fluctuating code anteriorly was predicted by the current simulations, using a model validated against neuropsychological, anatomical, and brain-imaging results in prior work.
source: Third, the observed pattern of a stable code posteriorly and fluctuating code anteriorly was predicted by the current simulations, using a model validated against neuropsychological, anatomical, and brain-imaging results in prior work (Patterson et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results and a citation to prior work (Patterson et al., 2007).

claim: Prior studies applying temporal generalization to MEG data in visual semantic tasks uniformly report a very narrow and unchanging band of temporal generalization.
source: Prior studies applying temporal generalization to MEG data in visual semantic tasks uniformly report a very narrow and unchanging band of temporal generalization (Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014), a pattern consistent with the proposal that the neuro-semantic code changes rapidly over the course of stimulus processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior MEG studies (Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014).

claim: The current results differ from the MEG pattern in showing a gradual widening of the temporal generalization window.
source: Our results differ from the MEG pattern, and indeed from most other work applying the temporal generalization approach (King and Dehaene, 2014), in showing a gradual widening of the temporal generalization window.
evidence: The claim compares the current findings to prior MEG studies.

claim: The widening of the temporal generalization window does not arise from the autocorrelational structure of the data itself.
source: This phenomenon does not arise from the autocorrelational structure of the data itself—the window of time over which an electrode reliably predicts its own future state does not grow wider with stimulus processing (A-5).
evidence: The claim is supported by additional analysis described in Appendix A-5.

claim: The widening of the temporal generalization window must reflect an increasingly stable representational code.
source: Instead the widening must reflect an increasingly stable representational code.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the analysis of temporal generalization.

claim: Hub representations in vATL change rapidly early on due to interactions with modality-specific representations throughout cortex, but these changes slow as the full activation pattern emerges across network components.
source: The simulation explains why the pattern arises in anterior temporal cortex: hub representations in vATL change rapidly early on due to interactions with modality-specific representations throughout cortex, but these changes slow as the full activation pattern emerges across network components.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Animacy is a useful starting point for studying semantic representation because it is not transparently captured by low-level perceptual structure.
source: Animacy is a useful starting point because it is not transparently captured by low-level perceptual structure; in our stimuli, for instance, low-level visual similarity as expressed by Chamfer matching does not reliably distinguish the animate and inanimate items (see Materials and Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by the Chamfer matching analysis described in Materials and Methods.

claim: Low-level visual similarity as expressed by Chamfer matching does not reliably distinguish the animate and inanimate items in the study stimuli.
source: Animacy is a useful starting point because it is not transparently captured by low-level perceptual structure; in our stimuli, for instance, low-level visual similarity as expressed by Chamfer matching does not reliably distinguish the animate and inanimate items (see Materials and Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by the Chamfer matching analysis described in Materials and Methods.

claim: It remains possible that decoders in the current work exploit some other property that happens to be confounded with animacy.
source: Nevertheless it remains possible that decoders in the current work exploit some other property that happens to be confounded with animacy.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: Whether decoders exploit animacy or some confounded property, the relevant information is expressed in a distributed, dynamically-changing neural code.
source: Whether this is the case or not, the preceding arguments suggest that the relevant information is expressed in a distributed, dynamically-changing neural code.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the overall findings.

claim: Common unsupervised methods like representational similarity analysis can yield a positive result even if the signal or target truly encodes just a binary label.
source: Common unsupervised methods like representational similarity analysis—where one computes the correlation between neural and target dissimilarity matrices—don't fit the bill, because such correlations can yield a positive result even if the signal or target truly encodes just a binary label (as shown, e.g., in 45), and can yield a negative result if a signal is present but buried in amongst many irrelevant features (Cox and Rogers, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Cox and Rogers, 2021).

claim: Representational similarity analysis can yield a negative result if a signal is present but buried in amongst many irrelevant features.
source: Common unsupervised methods like representational similarity analysis—where one computes the correlation between neural and target dissimilarity matrices—don't fit the bill, because such correlations can yield a positive result even if the signal or target truly encodes just a binary label (as shown, e.g., in 45), and can yield a negative result if a signal is present but buried in amongst many irrelevant features (Cox and Rogers, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Cox and Rogers, 2021).

claim: Generative approaches to decoding are problematic because they assume that each element of the neural code is independent.
source: "Generative" approaches (e.g.Pereira et al., 2018 )—where one predicts the neural response at each electrode from a feature-based description of the stimulus—are problematic because they assume that each element of the neural code is independent (ie, the "meaning" of a voltage deflection at a given electrode is the same regardless of the states of other electrodes).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Pereira et al., 2018) and represents a critique of that approach.

claim: Oswal et al., 2016 recently developed theory and analysis for a multivariate decoding approach tailored to the decoding of neural data that predicts the embedding of stimuli within a multidimensional semantic space.
source: Oswal et al., 2016 recently developed theory and analysis for such an approach tailored to the decoding of neural data, and future work should consider whether more continuous/fine-grained aspects of semantic similarity can be decoded from vATL using such techniques.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Oswal et al., 2016).

claim: Voltages measured at a surface electrode can be influenced by firing of nearby neurons but also by the activity of incoming synapses from neural populations at varying distances from the recording sites.
source: Voltages measured at a surface electrode can be influenced by firing of nearby neurons but also by the activity of incoming synapses from neural populations at varying distances from the recording sites.
evidence: The claim represents knowledge about ECoG signal sources.

claim: There is no guarantee that signals measured in vATL only reflect neural activation arising in vATL.
source: Thus there is no guarantee that signals measured in vATL only reflect neural activation arising in vATL.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the nature of ECoG signals.

claim: Power in the gamma band is often thought to reflect spiking activity of local neurons.
source: Power in the gamma band is often thought to reflect spiking activity of local neurons (Merker, 2013), and thus might provide a better indication of the activity of neurons within vATL proper.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Merker, 2013).

claim: Neural network models of semantic cognition do not exhibit oscillating behavior.
source: First, our goal was to assess whether the neural code for animacy has the distributed and dynamic properties that arise within a well-studied neural network model of semantic cognition. Such models do not exhibit oscillating behavior, making the model analog to frequency bands unclear.
evidence: The claim represents knowledge about neural network models.

claim: Prior ECoG work has shown that, while object- and person-naming does elicit increased gamma for more perceptual areas (like posterior fusiform), in anterior temporal regions it significantly alters beta-band power.
source: Prior ECoG work has shown that, while object- and person-naming does elicit increased gamma for more perceptual areas (like posterior fusiform), in anterior temporal regions it significantly alters beta-band power (Abel et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Abel et al., 2016).

claim: Tsuchiya et al., 2008 applied multivariate decoding to ECOG signals to discriminate happy and fearful faces, finding reliable information in ventral temporal cortex in frequencies < 30 Hz (as well as in gamma).
source: Similarly, (Tsuchiya et al., 2008) applied multivariate decoding to ECOG signals to discriminate happy and fearful faces, finding reliable information in ventral temporal cortex in frequencies < 30 Hz (as well as in gamma).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Tsuchiya et al., 2008).

claim: Beta-band oscillations are thought to aid in coordination of long-distance neural interactions.
source: Such patterns may reflect ATL's connections to multiple distal cortical areas, since beta-band oscillations are thought to aid in coordination of long-distance neural interactions (Kopell et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Kopell et al., 2000).

claim: The current data do not address important questions about the role of parietal, frontal and lateral/superior-temporal systems in semantic processing.
source: The current data do not, for instance, address important questions about the role of parietal, frontal and lateral/superior-temporal systems in semantic processing.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: vATL is situated at the top of the ventral visual stream, but also connects directly to core language areas.
source: The area is situated at the top of the ventral visual stream, but also connects directly to core language areas (Nobre et al., 1994; Mesulam, 1998) and, via middle temporal gyrus, to parietal areas involved in object-directed action (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Nobre et al., 1994; Mesulam, 1998; Chen et al., 2017).

claim: vATL receives direct input from smell and taste cortices.
source: It receives direct input from smell and taste cortices (Gloor, 1997), and is intimately connected with limbic structures involved in emotion, memory, and social cognition (Gloor, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gloor, 1997).

claim: vATL is intimately connected with limbic structures involved in emotion, memory, and social cognition.
source: It receives direct input from smell and taste cortices (Gloor, 1997), and is intimately connected with limbic structures involved in emotion, memory, and social cognition (Gloor, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gloor, 1997).

claim: vATL anatomically forms the hub of a cross-modal network ideal for encoding associations among visual, linguistic, action, sensory, and social/motivational representations.
source: Thus vATL anatomically forms the hub of a cross-modal network ideal for encoding associations among visual, linguistic, action, sensory, and social/motivational representations.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the anatomical connectivity of vATL.

claim: Hub neurons interact with a wide variety of subsystems, each encoding a different kind of structure and content, potentially pushing the hub representations in different directions over time as activity propagates in the network.
source: Hub neurons interact with a wide variety of subsystems, each encoding a different kind of structure and content, potentially pushing the hub representations in different directions over time as activity propagates in the network.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the dynamics of hub representations.

claim: Other network components lying closer to the sensory or motor periphery connect mainly within individual modality-specific systems.
source: Other network components lying closer to the sensory or motor periphery connect mainly within individual modality-specific systems (Binney et al., 2012), so may be less impacted by such cross-modal interactions, as observed in the model.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Binney et al., 2012) and inference from the model.

claim: The feature-based approach that has proven indispensable for characterizing neural representations in modality-specific cortices may be less suited to understanding the distributed and dynamic representations that arise in deeper and more broadly-connected (tertiary association) cortical regions.
source: For this reason, the feature-based approach that has proven indispensable for characterizing neural representations in modality-specific cortices may be less suited to understanding the distributed and dynamic representations that arise in deeper and more broadly-connected (tertiary association) cortical regions.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Tertiary association cortices may adopt dynamic distributed codes difficult to detect with common brain imaging methods.
source: These include regions critical for human semantic knowledge, and potentially other higher-level cognitive functions.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the overall findings of the study, as stated in the abstract.

claim: The model implements the 'distributed-plus-hub' theory of semantic representation developed in prior work.
source: The model implements the 'distributed-plus-hub' theory of semantic representation developed in prior work (Patterson et al., 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Rogers et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Patterson et al., 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Rogers et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2017).

claim: All units in the model employed a continuous-time sigmoidal activation function with a time-constant of 0.25.
source: All units employed a continuous-time sigmoidal activation function with a time-constant of 0.25.
evidence: The claim describes a parameter of the computational model.

claim: Visual and Verbal units in the model were given a fixed, untrainable bias of –3 that produced a low activation state without positive input.
source: Visual and Verbal units were given a fixed, untrainable bias of –3 that produced a low activation state without positive input.
evidence: The claim describes a parameter of the computational model.

claim: To simulate perception of an image, units encoding the item's visual representation were given direct positive stimulation of +6.
source: To simulate perception of an image, units encoding the item's visual representation were given direct positive stimulation of +6 so that, combined with the fixed bias, they received a net input of +3 (in addition to any inputs from other units in the model) which persisted through stimulus processing.
evidence: The claim describes the simulation procedure for the model.

claim: Units in the model updated their activation states asynchronously in permuted order on each tick of time.
source: Units updated their activation states asynchronously in permuted order on each tick of time and were permitted to settle for five time intervals (a total of 20 updates) during training and eight time intervals (32 updates) during testing.
evidence: The claim describes the update procedure for the model.

claim: Visual patterns in the model were constructed to represent each item by randomly flipping the bits of a binary category prototype vector.
source: Visual patterns were constructed to represent each item by randomly flipping the bits of a binary category prototype vector in which items from the same domain shared a few properties and items from the same category shared many.
evidence: The claim describes the construction of training data for the model.

claim: Verbal patterns in the model were constructed by giving each item a superordinate label, a basic-level label, and a subordinate label.
source: The verbal patterns were constructed by giving each item a superordinate label true of all items within a given domain (animal, object, plant), a basic-level label true of all items within a category (e.g. 'bird', 'fish', 'flower', etc), and a subordinate label unique to the item (e.g. 'robin', 'salmon', 'daisy', etc).
evidence: The claim describes the construction of training data for the model.

claim: The model was trained with backpropagation to minimize squared error loss.
source: The model was trained with backpropagation to minimize squared error loss.
evidence: The claim describes the training procedure for the model.

claim: Half of the training patterns involved generating verbal outputs from visual inputs, while the other half involved generating visual outputs from verbal inputs.
source: Half of the training patterns involved generating verbal outputs from visual inputs, while the other half involved generating visual outputs from verbal inputs.
evidence: The claim describes the training procedure for the model.

claim: The model was initialized with small random weights sampled from a uniform distribution ranging from –1–1, then trained for 30,000 epochs in full batch mode with a learning rate of 0.002 and without weight decay.
source: The model was initialized with small random weights sampled from a uniform distribution ranging from –1–1, then trained for 30,000 epochs in full batch mode with a learning rate of 0.002 and without weight decay.
evidence: The claim describes the training procedure for the model.

claim: After training, all models generated correct output activations for more than 99% of output units across all training runs.
source: For all reported simulations, the model was trained five times with different random weight initializations. After training, all models generated correct output activations (i.e. on the correct side of the unit midpoint) for more than 99 % of output units across all training runs.
evidence: The claim describes the performance of the trained model.

claim: Eight patients with intractable partial epilepsy (seven) or brain tumor (one) originating in the left hemisphere participated in the ECoG study.
source: Eight patients with intractable partial epilepsy (seven) or brain tumor (one) originating in the left hemisphere participated in this study.
evidence: The claim describes the participants in the ECoG study.

claim: Subdural electrode implantation was performed in the left hemisphere for presurgical evaluation (mean 83 electrodes, range 56–107 electrodes/patient).
source: Subdural electrode implantation was performed in the left hemisphere for presurgical evaluation (mean 83 electrodes, range 56–107 electrodes/patient).
evidence: The claim describes the electrode implantation procedure.

claim: A total of 16–24 electrodes (mean 20 electrodes) covered the ventral ATL in each patient.
source: A total of 16–24 electrodes (mean 20 electrodes) covered the ventral ATL in each patient.
evidence: The claim describes the electrode coverage in the ECoG study.

claim: The subdural electrodes were constructed of platinum with an inter-electrode distance of 1 cm and recording diameter of 2.3 mm.
source: The subdural electrodes were constructed of platinum with an inter-electrode distance of 1 cm and recording diameter of 2.3 mm (ADTECH, WI).
evidence: The claim describes the electrode specifications.

claim: ECoG recording with subdural electrodes revealed that all epilepsy patients had seizure onset zone outside the anterior fusiform region, except one patient for whom it was not possible to localize the core seizure onset region.
source: ECoG recording with subdural electrodes revealed that all epilepsy patients had seizure onset zone outside the anterior fusiform region, except one patient for whom it was not possible to localize the core seizure onset region.
evidence: The claim describes the clinical characteristics of the patients.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Kyoto University Graduate School of Medicine (No. C533).
source: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Kyoto University Graduate School of Medicine (No. C533).
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: One hundred line drawings were obtained from previous norming studies, including 50 items in each of the two semantic categories (animal vs non-animal).
source: One hundred line drawings were obtained from previous norming studies (Barry et al., 2018; Snodgrass and Vanderwart, 1980), including 50 items in each of the two semantic categories that were the target of our decoding efforts (animal vs non-animal).
evidence: The claim describes the stimuli used in the ECoG study and is supported by citations to prior work (Barry et al., 2018; Snodgrass and Vanderwart, 1980).

claim: Living and nonliving stimuli were matched on age of acquisition, visual complexity, familiarity and word frequency, and had high name agreement.
source: Living and nonliving stimuli were matched on age of acquisition, visual complexity, familiarity and word frequency, and had high name agreement.
evidence: The claim describes the stimulus matching procedure.

claim: Independent-sample t-tests did not reveal any significant differences between living and nonliving items for any of the matched variables.
source: Independent-sample t-tests did not reveal any significant differences between living and nonliving items for any of these variables.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical analysis of stimulus matching.

claim: Mean accuracy across folds for decoding living/nonliving from Chamfer matching similarities was 0.51 and did not differ reliably from chance.
source: Mean accuracy across folds was 0.51 and did not differ reliably from chance, indicating that the animal/non-animal distinction is not readily discernable solely from the non-semantic visual structure of the images.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Chamfer matching analysis.

claim: Participants' mean naming time was 1190 ms.
source: Participants' mean naming time was 1190 ms.
evidence: The claim describes the behavioral data from the ECoG study.

claim: Raw data were recorded at sampling rate of 1000 Hz for six patients and at 2000 Hz for two patients.
source: Raw data were recorded at sampling rate of 1000 Hz for six patients and at 2000 Hz for two patients.
evidence: The claim describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: The higher sampling rates for the two patients were down-sampled to 1000 Hz by averaging measurements from each successive pair of time-points.
source: The higher sampling rates for the two patients were down-sampled to 1000 Hz by averaging measurements from each successive pair of time-points.
evidence: The claim describes the data preprocessing procedure.

claim: Baseline correction was performed by subtracting the mean pre-stimulus baseline amplitude (200 ms before picture onset) from all data points in the epochs.
source: Baseline correction was performed by subtracting the mean pre-stimulus baseline amplitude (200 ms before picture onset) from all data points in the epochs.
evidence: The claim describes the data preprocessing procedure.

claim: Trials with greater than±500 µV maximum amplitude were rejected as artifacts.
source: Trials with greater than±500 µV maximum amplitude were rejected as artifacts.
evidence: The claim describes the artifact rejection procedure.

claim: The classifiers in the ECoG study were logistic regression models fitted with L1 regularization using the glmnet function in Matlab.
source: The classifiers were logistic regression models fitted with L1 regularization (Tibshirani, 1996) using the glmnet function in Matlab.
evidence: The claim describes the classifier methodology and is supported by a citation to prior work (Tibshirani, 1996).

claim: L1-regularization applies an optimization penalty that scales with the sum of the absolute value of the classifier coefficients and thereby encourages solutions in which many features receive coefficients of 0.
source: L1-regularization applies an optimization penalty that scales with the sum of the absolute value of the classifier coefficients and thereby encourages solutions in which many features receive coefficients of 0.
evidence: The claim describes the properties of L1 regularization.

claim: Classifier accuracy for a given time-window and subject was assessed using nested 10-fold cross-validation.
source: Classifier accuracy for a given time-window and subject was assessed using nested 10-fold cross-validation.
evidence: The claim describes the cross-validation procedure.
